_comment: The whole voiceover script. Each scene is a list of lines; each line is one caption and one voice clip. `speech` (optional) is what the voice says when it should differ from the caption. `pad` (optional) adds extra seconds after the line so an animation can finish. Scene ids must match SCENE_COMPONENTS in src/GanVideo.tsx.

lines.text: Imagine a computer that can invent faces of people who have never existed.
That is what a generative adversarial network, or GAN, can do.
Its trick: two neural networks that compete against each other.
Most neural networks you meet are classifiers: an image goes in, a label comes out.
A generative model runs the other way: random numbers go in, brand-new data comes out.
The goal is new samples that look like they came from the training data.
But how do you score a made-up picture? There is no right answer to compare it with.
The GAN's answer: train a second network to be the judge.
Think of a forger making fake banknotes, and a detective trying to catch them.
At first the fakes are terrible, and the detective spots every one.
The forger learns from each failure, and the fakes get better.
So the detective has to get sharper too.
Each pushes the other, until the fakes can't be told apart from real money.
In a GAN, the forger is the generator, G, and the detective is the discriminator, D.
The generator takes a random noise vector z, and turns it into a fake sample, G(z).
lines.speech: The generator takes a random noise vector, zee, and turns it into a fake sample, G of zee.

lines.text: The discriminator is shown real samples from the training set, and fakes from the generator.
For each one, it outputs a single number: the probability that the input is real.
That verdict is the generator's only teacher. It never sees a real image itself.
The generator's input is just noise: for example, 100 random numbers from a bell curve.
lines.speech: The generator's input is just noise: for example, a hundred random numbers from a bell curve.

lines.text: Layer by layer, transposed convolutions grow it into an image, doubling its size each step.
Every z gives a different output. The space of all z's is called the latent space.
lines.speech: Every zee gives a different output. The space of all zees is called the latent space.

lines.text: Move smoothly from one z to another, and the output changes smoothly too.
lines.speech: Move smoothly from one zee to another, and the output changes smoothly too.

lines.text: The discriminator is an ordinary classifier, usually a CNN.
It shrinks the image, layer by layer, down to a single number.
A sigmoid squashes that number into the range 0 to 1: near 1 means real, near 0 means fake.
lines.speech: A sigmoid squashes that number into the range zero to one: near one means real, near zero means fake.

lines.text: The twist: its opponent keeps getting better, so its job never gets easier.
The contest is written as a single value function, V of D and G.
The first term rewards D for scoring real data close to 1.
lines.speech: The first term rewards D for scoring real data close to one.

lines.text: The second term rewards D for scoring the fakes close to 0.
lines.speech: The second term rewards D for scoring the fakes close to zero.

lines.text: D tries to make V as large as possible. G tries to make it small, by pushing D(G(z)) toward 1.
lines.speech: D tries to make V as large as possible. G tries to make it small, by pushing D of G of zee toward one.

lines.text: In practice G maximizes log D(G(z)) instead: same goal, but much stronger gradients while its fakes are still bad.
lines.speech: In practice, G maximizes log D of G of zee instead: same goal, but much stronger gradients while its fakes are still bad.

lines.text: Training alternates between the two players.
Step one: freeze G. Show D real samples labeled 1 and fakes labeled 0, and update D.
lines.speech: Step one: freeze G. Show D real samples labeled one, and fakes labeled zero, and update D.

lines.text: Step two: freeze D. Make fresh fakes, and this time label them as real.
The error flows back through D into G, but only G's weights change.
Repeat thousands of times.
This is a real GAN, trained by the code in this project, on numbers instead of images.
The real data, in green, has two bumps. The generator's samples, in pink, start as one narrow spike.
The blue curve is the discriminator: how likely it thinks each value is to be real.
Where D says real, G moves its samples. Where D says fake, G moves away.
The spike spreads out, then splits in two, until it matches the real data.
Now D is about one half wherever the data lives: it can no longer tell real from fake.
Only in the empty gap between the bumps can it still catch the few fakes left there.
Theory explains that ending.
For a fixed generator, the best discriminator is the share of real data at each point.
Plugging it back in, G is minimizing the Jensen–Shannon divergence: a distance between the two distributions.
lines.speech: Plugging it back in, G is minimizing the Jensen-Shannon divergence: a distance between the two distributions.

lines.text: Its minimum is reached exactly when the generator's distribution equals the data's. Then D is ½ everywhere.
lines.speech: Its minimum is reached exactly when the generator's distribution equals the data's. Then D is one half everywhere.

lines.text: The discriminator's loss is then 2 log 2, about 1.39. Our GAN finished at 1.38.
lines.speech: The discriminator's loss is then two log two, about one point three nine. Our GAN finished at one point three eight.

scenes.title: Why GANs are hard to train

lines.text: In practice, GANs are famously hard to train.
Mode collapse: G finds a few outputs that fool D, and makes only those. Here it covers just one bump.
Instability: instead of settling down, the two players can chase each other in circles.
Vanishing gradients: if D wins too easily, G gets almost no signal to learn from.
Fixes include better losses like the Wasserstein GAN, and careful architectures and normalization.
Ian Goodfellow and his colleagues introduced GANs in 2014.
DCGAN made them convolutional and stable. CycleGAN turned horses into zebras without paired examples.
Progressive growing, BigGAN and StyleGAN pushed them to photorealistic, high-resolution images.
Diffusion models now lead image generation, but adversarial training lives on in fast generators, upscalers and image tokenizers.
So, a GAN is two networks playing a game.
The generator turns noise into samples. The discriminator judges real versus fake.
They take turns improving, until the fakes are indistinguishable from the real data.
